description: Mature and regenerating axolotl limb connective tissue cells studied as the biological subject in which segment-specific positional information and chromatin-based encoding were examined during limb regeneration.
The regenerating limb tissue of salamander/axolotl used as the broader biological context for segment restoration and positional identity during regeneration.
The regenerative process by which missing limb segments are restored; central process under investigation for its chromatin-level control and segment-specific programming.
Segment-specific identity information encoded in connective tissue cells that guides correct limb segment regeneration and determines where structures should reform.
Genome-wide analysis of chromatin state used to identify segment-specific chromatin marks and regulatory element activity in mature and regenerating axolotl limb cells.
A repressive histone modification identified as the major positional mark with segment-specific levels in axolotl limb connective tissue cells, especially at homeoprotein gene loci.
Genomic loci of limb homeoprotein genes that show segment-specific enrichment of H3K27me3 and contribute to the intrinsic segment information code.
Regulatory genes or elements upstream of limb homeoprotein loci that were noted not to carry the same segment-specific H3K27me3 pattern as the loci themselves.
The chromatin-level encoding of segment identity inferred from segment-specific histone H3K27me3 patterns, proposed to store positional information intrinsically in connective tissue cells.
Regulatory DNA elements that become active during regeneration before developmental regulatory elements reappear, indicating regeneration-specific gene control.
Regulatory elements associated with developmental programs that reappear after regeneration-specific elements become active during limb regeneration.
A homeoprotein gene in the hand whose permissive chromatin state engages with the regeneration program and bypasses the upper limb program.
An open or permissive chromatin configuration at HoxA13 associated with activation of regeneration-related gene programs in the hand.
The gene regulatory program activated during limb regeneration, including regeneration-specific regulatory elements and conserved transcriptional control.
A developmental program associated with upper limb identity that is bypassed in the hand during engagement of the regeneration program.
Comparative regenerative species used to identify shared regeneration regulatory elements and conserved transcription factor sets.
Regulatory elements associated with regeneration that were compared across species to identify a conserved core set.

entity_name: CORE SHARED SET OF TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
description: A conserved group of transcription factors shared among regenerative animals, supporting an ancient regeneration program.
An evolutionarily conserved regeneration mechanism inferred from shared regulatory elements and transcription factors across regenerative animals.

The adult axolotl limb tissue that is amputated and studied as the biological subject for regeneration. It serves as the source of connective tissue cells that undergo reprogramming during blastema formation and limb regeneration.

The mature axolotl tissue context in which blastema precursor cells were difficult to identify and isolate. It represents the uninjured adult limb tissue from which connective tissue cell heterogeneity was tracked.

A transient regenerative tissue formed after forelimb amputation in which progenitor cells accumulate prior to limb regeneration. It is the key regenerative endpoint and cellular state analyzed in the study.
Cells in the adult tissue that give rise to the blastema. They are the target population whose identity and isolation were previously difficult and whose transition was tracked molecularly.
A lineage-tracing method used to follow cell fate and ancestry during regeneration. In this study it was combined with scRNA-seq to molecularly track connective tissue cell transitions.

A single-cell transcriptomic assay used to profile gene expression at cellular resolution. It enabled molecular tracking of connective tissue cell heterogeneity and state transitions during blastema formation.
Abbreviation for single-cell messenger RNA sequencing, the transcriptomic measurement method used to resolve cell identities and molecular states during regeneration.
The diversity of mature connective tissue cell states in the uninjured adult limb. This heterogeneity is analyzed as cells transition toward a blastema progenitor state.
The regenerative cellular state reached by connective tissue cells during blastema formation. It reflects the transition from mature tissue identity to a progenitor-like state.

A staged molecular reprogramming program underlying the transition of connective tissue cells during regeneration. It describes the coordinated sequence of molecular changes leading to progenitor-state acquisition.
Connective tissue cell types present in the uninjured adult limb that undergo reversion during regeneration. They are the cellular population being reprogrammed toward a progenitor state.
The normal adult limb environment prior to amputation. It provides the baseline tissue setting from which connective tissue cells are sampled and compared to regenerative states.

A relatively homogeneous, developmentally plastic cellular state acquired by connective tissue cells during regeneration. It is characterized by progenitor-like properties and precedes blastema formation.
A developmental phenotype recapitulated by regenerating connective tissue cells. It indicates that adult cells revert toward an embryonic-like limb developmental program.
The capacity of connective tissue lineage cells to generate multiple cell fates. In this study it is a functional property regained during reprogramming toward the progenitor state.
The connective tissue lineage of cells tracked during regeneration. It is the lineage context in which multipotency and state transitions were observed.
The coordinated molecular and cellular changes that convert mature connective tissue cells into regenerative progenitor-like cells. It is the central biological process illuminated by the study.
The broader regenerative process by which the axolotl restores limb structure after amputation. It encompasses blastema formation, cell-state transitions, and tissue rebuilding.
The broader animal group to which the axolotl belongs. It provides the comparative biological context for the regeneration phenomenon described in the paper.

A highly regenerative urodele amphibian used as the primary biological subject in the study. It is contrasted with mammals and mouse models because it can rapidly activate protein synthesis after injury and regenerate limbs.
The scientific species name for the axolotl, representing the regenerative vertebrate model examined for injury-induced translational control and tissue regeneration.
A mammalian comparison model used to show that protein synthesis is not activated after non-regenerative digit amputation, highlighting species-specific regenerative differences.
A heterologous cellular system used to engineer and test axolotl mTOR (axmTOR), enabling functional assessment of the axolotl-specific kinase properties in a mammalian context.
The tissue-damaging perturbation that triggers the regenerative response and rapid activation of protein synthesis in the axolotl. It serves as the initiating context for translational remodeling.
A limb/digit injury scenario in the mouse that does not elicit protein synthesis activation, used as a non-regenerative comparison condition.
The regenerative biological endpoint observed in the axolotl following injury, dependent on rapid translational activation and mTORC1 signaling.
The broader regenerative outcome mediated by mTORC1 pathway activity and translational control in the axolotl, encompassing restoration of damaged tissue.
The early repair process orchestrated by the translatome and rapid protein synthesis after injury, described as a key functional consequence of the regenerative response.
The rapid translational process activated uniquely after injury in the axolotl, involving selective translation from pre-existing messenger RNAs and supporting regeneration.
Regulation of mRNA translation that is remodeled during injury response in the axolotl and mediated by mTORC1 signaling to support regeneration.
A cellular sensing process to which axolotl mTOR is unusually sensitive, contributing to its labile, rapidly activatable state and regenerative competence.
The upstream signaling pathway identified as a key mediator of tissue regeneration and translational control in the axolotl, linking nutrient sensing to protein synthesis.
The mTOR kinase protein whose sequence has expanded uniquely in urodele amphibians and whose axolotl form exhibits hypersensitive signaling properties.
The engineered axolotl mTOR variant expressed in human cells to test species-specific functional properties. It behaves as a hypersensitive kinase primed for rapid activation.
Messenger RNA-derived molecular species identified by polysome sequencing as selectively activated at the level of translation after injury, including antioxidant and ribosome-related transcripts.
Existing mRNA pool from which transcripts are selectively translated in response to injury, enabling rapid protein synthesis without requiring new transcription.
A class of transcripts/proteins selectively activated during the injury response, likely contributing to protection from oxidative stress during regeneration.
Translational machinery-related components whose transcripts are selectively activated after injury, supporting increased protein synthesis during regeneration.
A nutrient uptake process whose inhibition is sufficient to suppress tissue regeneration, indicating dependence of the regenerative program on amino acid availability.
A transcriptome-wide translational profiling method used to identify transcripts selectively activated at the level of translation in response to injury.
An experimental perturbation that blocks amino acid transport and is sufficient to inhibit tissue regeneration, demonstrating functional dependence on nutrient sensing.

A primary model organism for regeneration studied here as the main biological subject in which limb development and regeneration are analyzed, especially regarding apical-ectodermal-ridge-like cell states and regenerative programs.
A tetrapod reference population used in the comparative multi-species atlas to contextualize limb developmental cell states and AER-related biology.
A comparative mammalian species included in the multi-species atlas to support cross-species analysis of limb development and regeneration-related cell programs.
A comparative avian species included in the multi-species atlas for cross-species assessment of limb developmental programs and AER characteristics.
A comparative amphibian species included in the multi-species atlas to broaden the evolutionary comparison of limb development and regeneration-associated cell states.

A specialized limb-bud cell population central to limb development and regeneration; in this study, their presence, re-formation, and characteristic features are evaluated in axolotl and compared across species.
Cells proposed to resemble apical-ectodermal-ridge cells and potentially re-form during limb regeneration; they represent a key developmental/regenerative cell state under investigation.
The defining molecular and cellular features associated with apical-ectodermal-ridge identity, used here to determine whether axolotl cells match an AER-like state.

The collection of molecular components and regulatory elements associated with AER function; in axolotl mesoderm, part of this machinery is detected, indicating partial recapitulation of limb developmental programs.
A tissue compartment in the axolotl limb that displays part of the AER machinery, suggesting involvement in limb (re)growth and regenerative patterning.
The embryonic process of limb formation, used here as the developmental reference state for comparing AER-related cell programs across species.
The regenerative process by which limbs are re-formed after loss or injury; the study examines whether AER-like cells and developmental programs are recapitulated during this process in axolotl.
A regenerative growth program in axolotl limbs associated with partial presence of AER machinery in mesoderm, implying a role in rebuilding limb structures.
A single-cell transcriptomics analysis framework used to compare cell states across axolotl, human, mouse, chicken, and frog and to resolve AER-related questions.
A transcriptomic mapping method used to assess spatial organization of cells and confirm that axolotl limbs do not fully re-form AER cells during regeneration.

A regenerative developmental process in which a lost limb is replaced. It is the central biological phenomenon discussed in the article, compared with limb development, and examined across multiple animal groups and model amphibians.

The developmental process by which limbs form during organismal growth. It is used in the article as a comparative biological framework for understanding similarities and differences with limb regeneration.

Interacting cellular and tissue-level processes that contribute to regenerative patterning and outgrowth during limb regeneration. The article highlights recent progress in understanding these interactions as a mechanistic component of regeneration.
A model amphibian species used to study tetrapod limb regeneration. Newts are highlighted as one of the three amphibian models in which limb regeneration has been investigated.
A model amphibian species used to study tetrapod limb regeneration. Axolotls are a key experimental organism in regeneration research and are specifically named in the focus article.
A model amphibian group used in studies of tetrapod limb regeneration. Frogs are included among the three amphibian models discussed in the article.
The regenerative replacement of limbs in tetrapods. This is the specific regeneration context emphasized in the article and is studied through amphibian model systems.
An animal phylum referenced as one of the groups studied for limb regeneration. They provide comparative biological insight into regenerative mechanisms.
An animal phylum referenced as one of the groups studied for limb regeneration. They contribute comparative evidence for conserved or divergent regenerative mechanisms.
An animal phylum referenced as one of the groups studied for limb regeneration. They are included as part of the broader comparative context for regeneration research.
A broad taxonomic grouping of animals mentioned as the domain in which limb regeneration is observed. It provides the evolutionary scope for the article's discussion.
The regenerative appendage used as the biological subject of the study; limb amputation initiates the positional-memory and regeneration program being investigated.
The salamander species serving as the regenerative model organism in which posterior identity, positional memory, and limb regeneration circuitry are examined.
Anterior limb-derived cells that normally retain anterior positional identity and can be experimentally reprogrammed toward posterior memory during regeneration.
Posterior limb-derived cells that maintain posterior positional identity and contribute to regeneration by forming signaling centers after amputation.
The developmental memory of anterior or posterior identity that persists in limb cells over time and influences their regenerative behavior and signaling output.
The regenerative process triggered by limb amputation in which cells form signaling centers and restore limb structures, serving as the central biological context of the study.
A self-reinforcing regulatory circuit involving Hand2 and Shh that stabilizes posterior identity and supports persistence of positional memory.
The posterior cell-state program established during development and maintained during regeneration to preserve posterior positional information.
A transcription factor with residual developmental expression in posterior cells; it is sustained after regeneration and participates in the Hand2-Shh feedback loop.
A signaling center formed during regeneration that is induced by posterior identity and contributes to regenerative patterning and maintenance of posterior memory.
Sonic hedgehog signaling molecule that is induced during regeneration, acts upstream of Hand2 expression, and participates in the positive-feedback loop controlling posterior identity.
An experimentally induced regulatory circuit in anterior cells after transient Shh exposure that drives stable Hand2 expression and posterior-like memory.

entity_name: TRANSIENT EXPOSURE OF ANTERIOR CELLS TO SHH DURING REGENERATION
description: A short-term experimental exposure scenario in which anterior cells encounter Shh during the regenerative phase, used to reprogram positional memory.
The translational application context in which reprogramming positional memory and altering signaling outputs may be leveraged for regenerative design.

A vertebrate subject group discussed as a highly regenerative animal model in the context of appendage and limb regeneration. It serves as a comparative biological system for understanding regeneration mechanisms.
A mammalian model organism used in the review as an experimental and comparative subject for digit tip regeneration. It represents a less regenerative mammalian system relative to salamander/axolotl.
A salamander species highlighted as the champion of tetrapod limb regeneration. It is a key regenerative model used to identify fundamental molecular features of appendage regeneration.
A regenerative biological process in which distal digit tissue is restored after loss. In the text, it is specifically associated with the mouse as a mammalian regeneration model.

The broader biological process of regrowing lost appendages, including limbs and related structures. It is the central process reviewed in the paper and involves coordinated immune response, wound healing, proliferation, patterning, and differentiation.
A specialized form of appendage regeneration focused on restoring limbs. It is emphasized as a major regenerative capability in salamanders and axolotls.
A host biological process that must be balanced during regeneration. It is part of the coordinated response required for successful appendage regeneration.
A repair process occurring after tissue loss or injury that contributes to regeneration. The text identifies it as one of the key processes orchestrated during appendage regeneration.
Cellular expansion process required during regeneration to rebuild lost structures. It is listed as a core component of the regenerative program.
A developmental process that establishes correct spatial organization during regeneration. It is necessary for restoring proper structure and form in regenerated appendages.
The process by which cells acquire specialized identities during regeneration. It is part of the coordinated regenerative program described in the abstract.
The molecular-level mechanisms and features underlying regenerative capacity. The review focuses on these aspects to compare regenerative systems and identify common requirements.
A set of experimental approaches used to discover and analyze fundamental features of limb regeneration. These tools enable molecular and genomic investigation of regenerative biology.
The desired translational endpoint of improving human regenerative capacity or repair outcomes. The paper frames this as a long-term goal of comparative regeneration research.
The injury or tissue-loss event that triggers regenerative responses. It is the initiating condition that good regenerators respond to in the context of appendage regeneration.
Animals with strong regenerative capacity, used as a comparative population for understanding robust appendage regeneration mechanisms.
Animals with limited or weaker regenerative capacity, used as a comparative population to contrast with highly regenerative species.
The amphibian regeneration model studied in the paper. Axolotls are the biological subject in which limb regeneration and position-specific gene reactivation are examined.

The regenerative biological process by which axolotls restore amputated limbs. It is the central process under investigation and is linked to developmental gene re-expression, positional memory, and nerve-dependent activation.

The limb removal event that initiates the regeneration scenario. In this context, amputation serves as the triggering condition that leads to reactivation of Lmx1b and subsequent regeneration-related responses.

The anatomical tissue location where Lmx1b expression is maintained before amputation and where nerve factors are applied to reactivate gene expression. It represents the positional context relevant to dorsal identity and positional memory.

A position-specific developmental gene that determines limb dorsal identity in many animals. Its expression is maintained in intact dorsal skin and reactivated after amputation, making it a key molecular marker of positional memory and regeneration.
A class of genes re-expressed during limb regeneration that help reorganize developmental axes. They provide the molecular basis for restoring positional information during regeneration.
Genes whose expression reflects spatial identity within the limb. Their re-expression during regeneration is central to restoring correct positional patterning.
The retained tissue-level memory of spatial identity before amputation. It is proposed to be encoded by maintained Lmx1b expression and to instruct cells about their pre-amputation location.
The local presence of nerves in the regenerating limb environment. It is required for Lmx1b activation and functions as a permissive contextual factor for regeneration.
Nerve-derived signaling factors that can substitute for nerve presence in reactivating Lmx1b. They are experimentally applied to dorsal skin and include BMP2, FGF2, and FGF8.

A combined factor mixture consisting of BMP2, FGF2, and FGF8. This nerve-factor cocktail consistently reactivates Lmx1b when applied to dorsal skin and serves as the experimental intervention in the study.

A salamander model organism discussed as a highly regenerative vertebrate used to study limb regeneration mechanisms. It serves as the biological subject whose regenerative capacity motivates the paper's focus on molecular decoding.

A group of highly regenerative amphibians referenced as the broader comparative subject class. They are highlighted for their ability to spontaneously replace lost limbs and as a source of insight for regenerative medicine.
The human population is used as a comparative reference for limited natural regenerative ability. Humans are mentioned to emphasize translational relevance of salamander limb regeneration research.
A comparative mammalian population described as having limited natural abilities to regenerate lost body parts. This group provides the contrast that motivates studying salamander regeneration.

The biological process by which lost limbs are replaced, described as an astonishing regenerative capability in salamanders. It is the central process under investigation and the basis for regenerative medicine interest.
The molecular-level mechanisms that drive and regulate limb regeneration. The paper emphasizes that these mechanisms are being uncovered through new sequencing and functional approaches.

A translational biomedical endpoint and application area that could benefit from understanding salamander limb regeneration. It represents the broader clinical and therapeutic significance of the research.
The genomic content of salamanders, noted for its very large size and incomplete sequencing status. This molecular feature is presented as a major obstacle to molecular studies of regeneration.

Messenger RNA used as the starting molecular material for bridging the sequence-information gap in salamander studies. It enables transcript-based approaches when full genome sequences are unavailable.
Experimental approaches used alongside transcript-based data to investigate gene and pathway function in regeneration. It supports mechanistic inference about limb regeneration.
The body of genomic sequence data needed to study salamander biology at the molecular level. In the text, the lack of this information is described as a major barrier that has recently been bridged.

The amphibian model organism studied for its capacity to regenerate limbs and re-establish positional identity after injury. It serves as the biological subject in which proximalisation during regeneration is modeled.

The scientific species name for the axolotl, identifying the regenerative vertebrate model used in the study. It is the organism in which limb regeneration and proximal-distal patterning are examined.
The injury/exposure scenario initiating regeneration in the axolotl limb. It creates the wound context that triggers blastema formation and subsequent positional re-patterning.

The biological context in which cellular density, transfected cell distribution, and positional identity are tracked during regeneration. It represents the regenerative tissue environment along the proximal-distal axis.

A mass of progenitor cells that forms after limb amputation and drives regeneration by expanding and reconstructing distal structures. It is central to the regenerative process and positional memory maintenance.
Cells within the blastema that proliferate and contribute to rebuilding limb structures during regeneration. They are the cellular population whose distribution and progeny are tracked in the study.

The retained spatial identity information that mature cells near the wound are thought to preserve along the proximal-distal axis. It underlies the ability of regenerating tissue to reconstruct correct limb patterning.
The anatomical axis along which positional identity and cellular density are analyzed during limb regeneration. It provides the spatial framework for proximalisation and pattern reconstruction.
A key regulator of positional identity that promotes proximalisation when overexpressed. It is treated as a molecular factor influencing cell identity along the limb axis.
A key regulator of positional identity that promotes proximalisation when overexpressed. It functions as a molecular factor implicated in shifting cells toward proximal identity.
The shift of cells toward a more proximal positional identity during regeneration. It is the central biological process modeled in the study and is influenced by Prod1 and Tig1.
The positional state associated with more proximal limb characteristics. It is the identity state promoted by Prod1 and Tig1 and targeted during regeneration.
Distal blastema tissue that has been transfected with Tig1 and Prod1 for experimental manipulation. It represents the treated regenerative cell population used to study positional shifts.

The manipulated cells and descendant cells tracked over time to map spatial distribution during regeneration. They provide the cellular readout for assessing how transfection affects positional behavior.
The measured distribution of cells along the proximal-distal axis during regeneration. It is an observed endpoint used to characterize spatial changes after transfection.
The observed spatial and temporal pattern of transfected cells and their progeny throughout regeneration. It is a key outcome used to infer how positional identity evolves over time.
A continuous mathematical framework used to analyze regeneration dynamics and infer proximalisation behavior. It provides the analytical basis for estimating proximalisation velocity and force.
A modeled rate describing the speed of proximalisation induced by factors promoting proximal identity. It is a derived analytical quantity used to interpret the dynamics of positional change.

A modeled force-like quantity representing the driving influence behind proximalisation in the mathematical framework. It is linked to a positional potential and used to conceptualize directional identity change.
A modeled potential underlying the proximalisation force in the continuous mathematical framework. It represents the inferred directional landscape governing positional identity acquisition.

A tetrapod subject group used as the central comparative biological model in the paper. Salamanders are highlighted for their unique lifelong limb and tail regenerative capacity and for interspecies variation in development and regeneration.

The broader vertebrate population stratum used as the evolutionary context for comparing regenerative capacity. The text notes that among tetrapods, salamanders are exceptional in their ability to regenerate limbs and tails.

A regenerative anatomical endpoint discussed as the primary tissue structure that salamanders can restore throughout life. Limb regeneration is the central biological outcome motivating comparative analyses.

A regenerative anatomical endpoint mentioned alongside limbs as a tissue structure salamanders can regenerate throughout life. It serves as part of the organism-level regenerative phenotype under study.

The biological process of tissue restoration and regrowth after loss or injury. In this paper it refers specifically to salamander tissue regeneration, including limb and tail regeneration, and is the main mechanistic focus of comparative study.

A broader regenerative biological process encompassing restoration of damaged or lost tissues. The article frames comparative salamander studies as a way to understand mechanisms of tissue regeneration across species.
The specific regenerative process by which salamanders restore lost limbs. It is the title-level focus of the article and the key phenotype used to motivate comparative evolutionary analysis.
The genomic molecular resource of salamanders, described as large and newly being sequenced. These genomes provide the molecular basis for omics-enabled comparative studies of regeneration.

High-throughput molecular analysis methods used to integrate new perspectives into the study of tissue regeneration. They are presented as enabling technologies for comparative analyses of salamander regeneration.

A comparative research approach used to identify commonalities and differences in regeneration among salamander species. It functions as the analytical framework for evolutionary and mechanistic inference in the paper.
A comparative analytical concept referring to variation among salamander species in development and regeneration. It is used as evidence that regenerative capacity is not uniform across the group.

Paleontological evidence source used to infer ancestral characteristics and evolutionary context for salamander regeneration. Fossil data are cited as part of the comparative basis for understanding regeneration.
The vertebrate model organism discussed in the paper; salamanders are the subject in which limb regeneration is studied after amputation.
The initiating injury/scenario in which a limb is removed, triggering the regenerative response described in salamanders.
The immediate biological response to limb amputation that initiates downstream regenerative events leading to replacement of the missing limb part.
A regenerative cell mass formed after amputation that contains proliferating stem and progenitor cells and serves as the structure rebuilding limb tissues.
The cell population within the blastema that proliferates and contributes to regeneration of missing limb tissues.
A cell/tissue population recruited during regeneration that migrates to the wound site and contributes to blastema formation and tissue rebuilding.
Immune cell population involved in the regenerative response, migrating to the injury site as part of the coordinated cellular events after amputation.
Neuronal growth structures that participate in the regenerative process by migrating or extending toward the wound environment.
Mesenchymal-like tissue cells recruited during regeneration that contribute to blastema formation and limb tissue reconstruction.
The movement of multiple cell types to the wound site, a key coordinated process in blastema formation and limb regeneration.
Intercellular signaling and coordination among recruited cells that supports regenerative patterning and tissue rebuilding.
A physical-biological factor highlighted as part of the coordinated events influencing regeneration dynamics.
The process by which cells revert to a less differentiated, embryonic-like state during regeneration.
A dedifferentiated cell state resembling embryonic epithelial and mesenchymal cells, associated with regenerative plasticity.
The regenerative endpoint in which the amputated limb structure is restored.
The tissue-level regenerative outcome achieved through blastema-driven proliferation and coordinated cellular events.

The regenerative vertebrate model organism studied in the paper. It is the subject in which amputation-triggered body-wide and local responses are examined, with limb regeneration used as the key biological outcome.

The injury/exposure scenario that initiates the regenerative response. In this context it serves as the triggering event for both distant systemic activation and local tissue regrowth responses in axolotls.
Systemic responses occurring throughout the organism after injury rather than only at the wound site. The paper emphasizes these responses as previously underexplored and important for regeneration.

The autonomic nervous system component implicated in stimulating the systemic stem cell activation response to amputation. It functions upstream of adrenergic signaling in coordinating regeneration-related responses.

The signaling pathway mediating both distant cellular activation and local regeneration responses after amputation. It is described as coordinating systemic and local regenerative programs and acting upstream of mTOR signaling.
The body-wide activation of stem cells induced by amputation. This process is presented as a key regenerative priming event that contributes to enhanced limb regeneration.

Cellular activation occurring away from the injury site. These responses are coordinated by adrenergic signaling through the α2A-adrenergic receptor and represent the systemic component of the regenerative response.
Regenerative responses occurring at or near the injury site. These are coordinated by adrenergic signaling through β-adrenergic receptors and support localized tissue regrowth.
A receptor mediating adrenergic signaling in the distant/systemic arm of the regenerative response. It is specifically linked to coordination of distant cellular activation after amputation.
Receptors mediating adrenergic signaling in local regeneration responses. They are implicated in the localized regenerative program following amputation.
A downstream signaling pathway positioned after α2A- and β-adrenergic signaling in the regenerative cascade. It is described as being acted upon upstream by adrenergic signaling.
Axolotls that have undergone systemic activation in response to injury. This population is compared with naive animals and shows faster limb regeneration.
Axolotls lacking the systemic activation state described in the study. They serve as the comparison group for regeneration rate.
The regenerative endpoint measured in the study. It is enhanced by adrenergic/systemic activation and occurs faster in systemically activated axolotls than in naive animals.
A proposed foundational process in which cells throughout the body are primed for regeneration before localized tissue regrowth. The paper argues this is critical for enabling limb regeneration.
The local rebuilding of tissue at the injury site during regeneration. It is presented as the downstream regenerative consequence enabled by body-wide cellular priming.
An environmental context mentioned as a source of injury pressure in which enhanced regeneration may confer a selective advantage.
An environmental context of injury risk mentioned as a condition where faster regeneration may provide selective advantage.

A vertebrate model organism group used to study regeneration and immune involvement in tissue repair. In this text, salamanders are the primary subject population exhibiting broad regenerative capacity across multiple organs and appendages.

The biological process of restoring lost or damaged tissues and structures. Here it refers to salamander regenerative responses, including scar-free healing and faithful regrowth of complex organs and appendages.
A regenerative outcome characterized by tissue repair without fibrotic scar formation. It is highlighted as a hallmark of salamander regeneration and a desirable therapeutic endpoint.
An outcome in which lost structures are restored accurately in form and function. The text emphasizes this as part of the salamander regenerative repertoire across multiple tissues.

The host defense system implicated as a critical contributor to regenerative responses. In salamanders, immune components are observed at key stages of regeneration and are proposed to influence repair outcomes.
The rapid, non-specific arm of the immune response. The abstract notes that components of innate immunity are present during critical stages of salamander regeneration.
The antigen-specific arm of the immune response. The text indicates that adaptive immune components also participate in salamander regenerative stages.
Innate immune cells identified as functionally required during specific regenerative contexts. The text specifically mentions their requirement during heart and limb regeneration in salamanders.
The restoration of heart tissue after injury or loss. In salamanders, this process is cited as one of the regeneration contexts requiring macrophages.
The restoration of appendage structures after loss or injury. The abstract identifies this as another salamander regenerative process dependent on macrophages.
A complex organ that salamanders can regenerate substantially. It is listed among the tissues and organs capable of faithful regeneration.
A major organ that salamanders can regenerate. It is mentioned as part of the extensive regenerative repertoire and as a context in which macrophages are required.
A central nervous system organ included among salamander tissues capable of regeneration. It serves as an example of the breadth of regenerative capacity described.
A central nervous system structure that salamanders can regenerate. It is cited as one of the significant body parts restored during regeneration.
A craniofacial structure included in the salamander regenerative repertoire. The text notes that salamanders can regenerate significant parts of the jaws.
Respiratory structures that salamanders can regenerate. They are listed among the tissues and organs capable of faithful restoration.
Limb-like body structures that salamanders can regenerate throughout life. The text emphasizes whole appendage regeneration as a major feature of salamander biology.
A translational or clinical context in which insights from salamander regeneration may be applied. The abstract frames regenerative knowledge as potentially useful in such settings.
Experimental or comparative salamander-based models used to investigate regenerative biology and immune function. These models provide the evidence base for examining immunity in regeneration.
Comparative biological models used to generate insights relevant to regeneration and immunity. The text references them as sources of knowledge that may guide future salamander studies.
Genetic experimental methods proposed for revisiting prior observations and defining immune roles in regeneration. These approaches are suggested as tools to refine mechanistic understanding.

A regenerative biological process in which salamander limbs are rebuilt after injury. It is the central context of the review and is discussed as involving epithelial-mesenchymal transition, wound closure, blastema formation, stem cell activation, and possible fibrosis when regulation is aberrant.

A cellular transition program in which epithelial cells acquire mesenchymal-like properties. In this text it is proposed as a key regulator during multiple stages of salamander limb regeneration and is linked to cell migration, invasion, and potentially fibrosis.

Gene expression programs resembling epithelial-mesenchymal transition. They are hypothesized to regulate regenerative cellular behaviors in salamanders, especially in non-epithelial blastemal progenitor cells.
A salamander model organism used to study limb regeneration. The text identifies axolotls as one of the species in which EMT-related roles during regeneration are considered.
Additional salamander species beyond axolotls that serve as comparative regenerative models. They are included as the broader subject population for the proposed EMT-related mechanisms.
Movement of keratinocytes during wound repair. In this abstract it is proposed as one of the main cellular processes regulated by EMT during limb regeneration, specifically during wound closure.
The repair process that seals the injury site after limb amputation or damage. It is described as a stage of regeneration during which EMT may regulate keratinocyte migration.
A temporary cellular invasion into the amputated stump by epithelial cells undergoing EMT. It is presented as a proposed regenerative behavior during salamander limb regeneration.
Epithelial cells that are in the process of epithelial-mesenchymal transition. They are described as transiently invading the stump during regeneration.
Progenitor cells within the blastema that are not epithelial in origin. The text proposes that they may use EMT-like programs to escape their niches during regeneration.
Progenitor cells associated with the blastema, the regenerative cell mass in salamanders. They are implicated as potential users of EMT-like programs in the review.
Molecular regulators that may control EMT through nontraditional mechanisms during regeneration. They are mentioned as a topic warranting further investigation.
Activation of stem cells during regeneration. The review proposes this as a nontraditional role potentially linked to EMT during limb regeneration.
Pathological fibrotic tissue formation. In the abstract it is proposed as a possible consequence of aberrant EMT during limb regeneration.
Dysregulated or abnormal epithelial-mesenchymal transition. It is suggested to induce fibrosis if EMT regulation becomes improper during regeneration.

A regenerative vertebrate model organism used in this study to investigate limb regeneration and the molecular programs that enable appendage regrowth without scarring. It serves as the primary biological subject in which Tgf-β and Bmp signaling dynamics are examined.

The biological process of restoring lost appendages, emphasized here as the central regenerative phenomenon in axolotls. It is described as involving distinct phases, including preparation and redevelopment, and is regulated by Tgf-β and Bmp signaling.

A signaling family of molecular factors implicated in wound healing and developmental pattern formation. In this text, it is the broader molecular group targeted to understand its role in regeneration, including Tgf-β, Bmps, activins, and GDFs.

A member of the Tgf-β superfamily that is highlighted as important for the preparation phase of limb regeneration in axolotls. It is described as having a distinct temporal expression window and a non-canonical pathway that is not active during redevelopment.

Bone morphogenetic proteins, a sub-family of the Tgf-β superfamily that are emphasized as important for the redevelopment phase of limb regeneration. They are described as acting in a distinct window from Tgf-β and not overlapping with it.

A sub-family within the Tgf-β superfamily mentioned as part of the broader signaling family relevant to wound healing and development. They are included as related molecular components but are not the main focus of the regeneration model.

Growth differentiation factors, listed as members of the Tgf-β superfamily. They are part of the molecular context of the signaling family discussed in relation to regeneration and developmental patterning.

A biological repair process in adults that is used here as a functional context for the Tgf-β superfamily. It provides a mechanistic link between signaling family activity and tissue repair responses.
A developmental biological process in which the Tgf-β superfamily is involved. It is cited as a key functional context for these signaling molecules beyond regeneration.
An early phase of limb regeneration in axolotls during which Tgf-β is described as important. It represents a distinct temporal stage in the regenerative program.
A later phase of limb regeneration in axolotls during which Bmps are described as important. It is distinct from the preparation phase and is characterized by non-overlapping signaling activity.
A signaling pathway associated with Tgf-β that is reported as not active during redevelopment in axolotls. It is relevant for understanding phase-specific signaling control during regeneration.

A temporal expression pattern describing how Tgf-β and Bmps are maintained in separate expression windows during regeneration. This concept underlies the proposed molecular model for phase-specific signaling.

A conceptual analytical framework proposed to explain how Tgf-β and Bmps maintain distinct expression windows during axolotl regeneration. It serves as the interpretive model for the observations summarized in the review.

A physical injury event described as a major cause of limb loss in the review. It functions as the initiating clinical context for amputation and subsequent regenerative research, and is relevant as a damaging endpoint rather than a radiation-specific exposure.

Surgical or traumatic removal of a limb or appendage, presented as a major biomedical burden and the condition that motivates limb regeneration studies. It is the central adverse endpoint discussed in relation to regenerative repair.

The broad animal population discussed as capable of forming and patterning limbs during embryogenesis. In the review, vertebrates serve as the comparative biological population for regeneration capacity across species.

Amorphous clusters of cells described as the developmental cellular substrate from which normal limbs can form and pattern during embryogenesis. They are relevant as the cellular population underlying limb development and potential regeneration.
A vertebrate animal group highlighted as proficient limb regenerators throughout life. They are a key comparative model for understanding robust appendage regeneration.

entity_name: SPECIES THAT DO NOT NORMALLY REGENERATE THEIR APPENDAGES
description: A comparative subject population representing animals with limited or absent natural appendage regeneration. These species are the target of efforts to stimulate regeneration.
The biomedical translational context in which limb regeneration research is framed. It represents the clinical and research setting where strategies to restore damaged limbs are pursued.
The broad biological process referenced as being informed by limb regeneration research. It is discussed as a fundamental implication of studying regenerative capacity across vertebrates.

entity_name: CELLULAR CONTROL OF GROWTH AND FORM
description: A developmental biological process involving regulation of tissue growth and morphogenesis throughout the body. The review notes that limb regeneration studies have implications for understanding this process.

The biological process of rebuilding missing or damaged limbs, which is the central topic of the review. It is discussed as a naturally occurring ability in some vertebrates and as a target for experimental augmentation in other species.
The observed degree of complete limb restoration, especially in rodent models where success has been modest. It serves as the main functional endpoint for evaluating regeneration strategies.
Experimental frog-based animal models used to test approaches for augmenting limb regeneration. They are part of the comparative vertebrate systems discussed in the review.
Experimental mammalian animal models used to evaluate limb regeneration interventions. They provide a more clinically relevant but generally less regenerative comparison system.
Manipulative genetic approaches used to augment limb regeneration in experimental models. They represent one class of interventions reviewed for their ability to stimulate repair.
Chemical or molecular interventions used to enhance limb regeneration. They are discussed as one of the major strategy classes tested in frog and mammalian models.
Interventions that alter bioelectric states or signaling to promote regeneration. They are highlighted as an emerging approach for augmenting limb repair.
Rodent experimental models used to assess whole limb repair. The review notes that regenerative success in these models has been modest to date.

Emerging experimental tools and strategies proposed as part of the near-term roadmap for regeneration research. They are positioned as enabling future progress in basic and clinical limb regeneration.

A vertebrate subject/population used as the biological context for studying limb regeneration ability and regeneration mechanisms. The text treats amphibians as the representative organism group in which organ regeneration phenomena are observed.

A subgroup of amphibians highlighted as the species group in which the accessory limb model helped identify limb regeneration inducers. They are relevant as a comparative regeneration model and a source of evidence for regeneration universality.

An alternative experimental system used to investigate early regulation of amphibian limb regeneration. It functions as a study method/model that enabled identification of limb regeneration inducers and supports cross-species regeneration research.

The biological process of regrowing a limb, presented as a representative form of organ regeneration in amphibians. It is the central process under investigation and is influenced by defined molecular signals in the text.

A broader regenerative biological process encompassing limb regeneration. The text frames limb regeneration as a representative phenomenon of this process and discusses mechanisms that may be universal across species.

The underlying biological mechanisms that govern regeneration responses across species. The review aims to clarify and generalize these mechanisms using insights from the accessory limb model and defined molecular inducers.

A wound-repair process that can be reprogrammed by defined molecules into an organ regeneration response. It serves as the baseline repair state that is transformed in the experimental context described.

Regenerative responses that result in organ-level, specifically limb-level, regeneration rather than ordinary wound healing. These responses are induced by the defined molecular combination in the text.

A defined combination of molecules that can transform skin wound healing into organ (limb) regeneration responses and initiate regeneration responses in some species. It functions as the key regenerative inducer set in the abstract.

Factors identified through the accessory limb model that promote or induce limb regeneration in urodele amphibians. The text presents them as biologically active agents relevant to regeneration control.

A broader comparative population category indicating that regeneration responses initiated by the defined molecules are not limited to one amphibian group. It supports the claim of cross-species applicability of regeneration mechanisms.
